newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey to further ease limits on wheat imports.
newsitem.headline: Turkey to further ease limits on wheat imports.

text.p: Turkey will temporarily ease its strict health clearance requirements for several diseases in its wheat imports, in an apparent intention to end a month-old dispute with its main grain supplier, the United States, a senior agriculture official said on Monday.

Muammaer Yasarbas, deputy general manager of the Protection and Quarantine Directorate of the agricultural ministry, said the government would not seek clearances for five grain diseases and would impose a 0.05-percent tolerance for two others.
"Only a requirement of 0.05 percent wil be sought in karnal bunt and ergot fungi," he told a seminar on wheat quality arranged by U.S. Wheat Associates.
"For five other diseases no clearance will be sought for a temporary period of time," he said.
He said ministry officials and a visiting delegation from the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) would meet in Ankara this week to find "common ground between Turkey and the United States."

Jonathan Jones, national export programme manager for USDA's Animal Plant and Health Inspection Service, and Roy Barrett, marketing specialist with USDA's Foreign Agriculture Service -- both attending the seminar -- arrived in Ankara at the weekend for talks with Turkish officials.
"We believe ergot (fungus) is more of a quality issue than a quarantine issue," Barrett told the seminar.
Turkey and the U.S. have been in disagreement since October, when Ankara held several U.S.-origin wheat cargoes for inspection against ergot fungus under its then zero-tolerance policy.
The U.S. government responded by suspending phytosanitary certificates for grain exports to Turkey, virtually halting all grain sales.
Jones said he expected the issue would be resolved during their meeting with Turkish officials.
But a U.S. embassy official said Turkey's move to ease restrictions was good but not sufficient.
"Unless we see the new Turkish regulation in printed form, I do not think the U.S. government will begin issuing export certificates to Turkey," he told Reuters.
Yasarbas said the new regulation would come out soon after members of the cabinet approved it, but added, "It is now in practice because we got a verbal order from the agriculture minister."
Local wheat prices have shot up by about 30 percent in the past month.
